approachQuestion.prompt: A value is an integer record or an ordered list record. Produce a deep copy: every output record must be newly allocated, integer payloads and list order must match the input, and no output record may be an input record. Examples: [3,[4]] copies to the same shape with new records throughout; [] copies to a new empty list record.
constraints: A value is either a signed 32-bit integer or an ordered list of values; lists may be empty.
The input is finite, acyclic, and has no shared subobjects. There are n total integer and list objects, including the root, with 1 ≤ n ≤ 100000; maximum nesting depth is h ≤ 1000.
Do not modify the input. Indexing a list, reading a tag, and integer comparisons take constant time.
The input has no shared records. Allocating a record takes constant time, and appending a child reference has amortized constant cost.

options.text: Serialize the entire value into an unambiguous token array, then parse that array into fresh records.
options.feedback: It can satisfy the copy contract, but the full temporary representation is removable.

options.text: Allocate only a new outer list and reuse the original child references.
options.feedback: For [[3]], both the child list and integer would still be input records.

options.text: Return the input directly because its values already match the desired output.
options.feedback: Even an integer record must have a distinct output identity.

options.text: For an integer allocate a new integer record. For a list allocate a new list record, recursively copy each child in order, and append that returned reference.
options.feedback: Each input record has one fresh counterpart, and parents link to the returned copies rather than original children.

feedback.reason: Allocate a new counterpart for every record, including each list.
details: Each visit allocates the output counterpart of its input record. Integer records are copied directly. A list creates one output list and fills it with the returned copied child references, processed one at a time. No serialized representation or source-to-copy map is built.

Allocate a new counterpart for every record, including each list. Reusing an original child reference would violate deep copy despite equal printed values. Process one child at a time and attach its returned copy.

“Allocate only a new outer list and reuse the original child references.”: For [[3]], both the child list and integer would still be input records.

“For an integer allocate a new integer record. For a list allocate a new list record, recursively copy each child in order, and append that returned reference.”: Each input record has one fresh counterpart, and parents link to the returned copies rather than original children.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze method-1 as described in the revealed method. Let n and h have the meanings in Q1. Use child indices and references without copying lists. Count active call frames; exclude input and returned output. There is no tail-call elimination. No hashing is used. All allocated copied records and their child-reference capacity belong to the returned output and are excluded. Choose the tightest worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair among the options.

feedback.reason: Each record is copied once; only active traversal frames remain outside output.
details: Every record is copied once. After excluding the fresh output structure, only pending calls and their cursors consume auxiliary storage.
“O(n) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: Nested calls remain active along a path; their storage must be counted.
“O(n²) time, O(h + 1) auxiliary space”: Each object is processed once without rescanning or copying its descendants.
“O(h + 1) time, O(h + 1) auxiliary space”: A shallow but wide input can still require inspecting every object.
